name: Heroic vs villainous face perception

lead: The heroic versus villainous framework holds that people read a face for two things: how attractive it is, and what kind of behaviour it seems to signal. A forum guide on looksmax.org argues that this perceived behaviour, separate from the 'looks axis', shapes how others adjust themselves around you.

The appearance payoff is strategic: the guide's author says people should 'play what you can and not what you want', meaning understand what your face exudes and use it, including to see which kinds of people you may appeal to. Academic research on first impressions from faces is a separate literature.

paras: Followers sort facial features, such as brow position, canthal tilt and eye hooding, into archetypes like a heroic 'knight' type or a darker 'villain' type, then compare their own face and adjust grooming, expression and style to lean into or soften the impression. Commenters in the thread debate which archetype particular features and named people belong to.

The categories are informal and contested, even among the thread's own participants. Reading character from facial structure is a long-running popular idea, and social-psychology texts note that people do form quick impressions from features, but the specific heroic/villainous mapping has not been tested in published studies.

angle.text: Proponents say knowing whether your face reads heroic or villainous lets you style and present it deliberately rather than fight it, and understand who you are likely to appeal to.

lead: Heroic vs villainous face perception is a framework from looksmaxxing forums for how facial structure is read as signalling safe, heroic, good behaviour or mysterious, villainous, bad behaviour. It was laid out in a looksmax.org guide titled 'Guide To Understanding Perceived Behaviours In Faces', which describes it as an unexplored but important topic for a looksmaxxer [1].

The guide's central claim is that observers read two things: a looks level, which affects how they treat you, and a perceived behaviour, which affects how they adjust themselves around you because of how they think you act. The author describes a 'looks axis' and many 'behavioral axes' and says the way a face looks defines its perceived behaviour [1].

How it helps someone look better is practical. The author says the aim is to understand what your face exudes and use it to your benefit, and to understand which girls you may appeal to, in line with the advice to play what you can rather than what you want [1]. Replies in the thread discuss which features place a face in a 'knight' section, such as low-set positive brows with neutral or positive canthal tilt and negative hooding [1].
infobox: Looks axis plus multiple behavioural axes

paras: The framework treats a face as sending a behavioural message in addition to an attractiveness score. Its author calls the second signal 'perceived behaviour' and says it is as important as looks level because it governs how people treat and adjust to you [1].

The guide groups features into archetypes along a heroic/safe/good to villainous/mysterious/bad range. Replies in the thread quarrel over which brow and canthal combinations belong in the 'knight' section and whether named examples fit it [1].

Readers are encouraged to apply it self-diagnostically: work out what your face exudes, then pick grooming, expression, clothing and social settings that suit it. The author presents this as complementary to ordinary looks improvement, not a replacement [1]. One commenter praised the thread as a useful read on facial archetypes [1].

A social-psychology overview notes that people judge strength and assertiveness from features such as an angular chin and low eyebrows, and associate baby-faced people with harmlessness [2]. This is a general finding about trait impressions from faces and does not use the heroic/villainous categories.
No studies found. Research on first impressions from faces exists as a broader category [2], but no published study has tested the heroic versus villainous framework.

lore.intro: The idea circulates mainly in one looksmax.org guide thread and its replies, where members sort faces into behavioural archetypes [1].

claims.claim: Faces carry a 'perceived behaviour' separate from attractiveness
